# Abstract

Between Stalin's death in March 1953 and the dissolution of the USSR in December 1991, the urban population of the seven western and northern union republics - the Russian SFSR and the Ukrainian, Byelorussian, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian and Moldavian SSRs - nearly doubled from 86,78M at the 1959 census to 156,78M in 1989. Alongside the steady growth of the republican capitals and older provincial centres, post-Stalin economic planning created hundreds of new towns: Volga, Dnieper and Angara-Yenisei hydroelectric cities, automotive and petrochemical monocities, Moscow science cities, closed nuclear and naval towns (*ZATO*) and Arctic oil, gas, diamond and railway settlements across West Siberia, Yakutia and the Baikal-Amur Mainline.

This gazetteer traces the population histories of 292 towns and urban settlements across all 41 regions from 1953 to 1991. Together with the four post-war Soviet censuses of 1959, 1970, 1979 and 1989 and the opening (1953) and closing (1991) benchmarks, the tables record the pre-evacuation populations of towns inside the 1986 Chernobyl Exclusion Zone and the declassified headcounts of the secret nuclear and naval cities omitted from contemporary Soviet publications.


# Methodology

The 292 settlements in this gazetteer span all 41 regions of the Estonian SSR (Region 1), Latvian SSR (Region 2), Lithuanian SSR (Region 3), Moldavian SSR (Region 4), the Kaliningrad Oblast RSFSR exclave (Region 5), the Byelorussian SSR (Regions 6-8), the Ukrainian SSR (Regions 9-15) and the mainland RSFSR (Regions 16-41) [@tssu_1962_perepis_1959; @tssu_1972_perepis_1970; @tssu_1984_perepis_1979; @goskomstat_1991_perepis_1989; @goskomstat_1992_demograficheskiy_ezhegodnik_1991]. Population figures are drawn from the All-Union census returns of January 1959, January 1970, January 1979 and January 1989, supplemented by TsSU and Goskomstat urban registers for 1953 and 1991, post-Soviet declassified *Minsredmash* series for closed nuclear and naval cities, and April 1986 pre-evacuation counts for settlements evacuated after the Chernobyl accident [@lappo_1997_geografiya_gorodov; @rowland_1996_russia_secret_cities_zato; @iaea_2006_chernobyl_environmental_consequences].

The regional tables in the Results section group the towns into four geographic zones: the 47 towns of the Baltic SSRs, the Moldavian SSR and Kaliningrad Oblast (Regions 1-5); the 82 towns of the Byelorussian and Ukrainian SSRs (Regions 6-15); the 107 towns of European Russia, the Volga-Ural republics and the North Caucasus (Regions 16-30); and the 56 towns of Siberia, Yakutia and the Far East (Regions 31-41). The Appendix then presents all 292 settlements in a single alphabetical directory with their full benchmark series.


# Results

## Baltic SSRs, Moldavian SSR and Kaliningrad Exclave

In the western borderlands (Regions 1-5), urban growth followed contrasting paths: heavy industrial migration into Tallinn, Riga, the Ida-Virumaa oil-shale basin and the left-bank Dniester towns of Tiraspol, Bender and Ribnita, balanced ten-pole regional urbanisation across Lithuania, and naval and fishing expansion in Kaliningrad Oblast (Table \ref{tab:western-ssrs-kaliningrad}).

## Byelorussian and Ukrainian SSRs

Across Belarus and Ukraine (Regions 6-15), post-war urban growth was led by Minsk, Kyiv, the western oblast capitals, the Dnieper hydroelectric and metallurgical bend and the Black Sea ports, while the April 1986 Chernobyl accident forced the evacuation of Pripyat, Chernobyl and Poliske and the construction of Slavutych (Table \ref{tab:belarus-ukraine}).

## European Russia, Volga-Urals and the North Caucasus

In the European RSFSR, the Volga-Ural republics and the North Caucasus (Regions 16-30), metropolitan expansion in Moscow and Leningrad, the Volga-Kama automotive and petrochemical boomtowns (Tolyatti, Naberezhnye Chelny, Nizhnekamsk and Volzhsky), the Ural closed nuclear towns and the restored capitals of Elista, Grozny, Nalchik and Cherkessk contrasted with rural contraction in the surrounding forest and black-earth villages (Table \ref{tab:european-russia}).

## Siberia, Yakutia and the Far East

East of the Urals (Regions 31-41), older Trans-Siberian and Kuzbass industrial cities were joined by the oil and gas boomtowns of the Middle Ob and Yamal (Surgut, Nizhnevartovsk, Nefteyugansk, Novy Urengoy, Noyabrsk and Nadym), the Angara-Yenisei hydroelectric cities (Bratsk, Angarsk, Ust-Ilimsk, Divnogorsk and Sayanogorsk), the diamond and coal towns of Yakutia (Mirny, Udachny and Neryungri) and the hubs of the Baikal-Amur Mainline and Pacific coast (Table \ref{tab:siberia-fareast}).

# Conclusion

Across the 292 settlements catalogued in this gazetteer, the post-Stalin decades marked the peak of Soviet urban and frontier expansion. Between 1953 and 1991, rural out-migration from the European forest and forest-steppe zones and state investment in automotive, hydroelectric, nuclear and hydrocarbon complexes created a dense hierarchy of regional capitals and specialised industrial towns. With the end of the USSR in December 1991 and the withdrawal of northern wage and transport subsidies, many Arctic mining towns and single-industry *monogoroda* entered demographic contraction, making the 1989-1991 benchmarks the historical high point of the late-Soviet urban network.
